In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Qasas

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We wished to confer favour upon those who were oppressed in the land, and to make them leaders, and to make them the inheritors﴾. We have already explained that His saying here, ﴿And We wished to confer favour upon those who were oppressed﴾, is the word referred to in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled upon the Children of Israel﴾ [al-A'raf: 137]. Here He did not state the reason for which He made them *a'immah* (plural of *imam*, meaning leaders), that is, leaders in goodness and callers to it, according to the more apparent of the two opinions. Nor did He state here the thing by which He made them its inheritors. However, He, may He be exalted, has clarified all of that in another place. He clarified the reason for which He made them leaders in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and were certain of Our signs﴾ [as-Sajdah: 24]. So patience and certainty are the cause of that. And He clarified the thing He made them inheritors of

• by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern regions of the land and its western regions﴾ [al-A'raf: 137],

• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How many gardens and springs did they leave behind, ﴿and crops and a noble station, ﴿and luxury in which they had been enjoying themselves. ﴿Thus, and We bequeathed them to another people﴾ [ad-Dukhan: 25–28],

• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We removed them from gardens and springs, ﴿and treasures and a noble station. ﴿Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 57–59].

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. Know that the verified view, God willing, is that the lām in His words ﴿for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8] is the lām of causation (lām al-ta'līl, known as lām kay), and that this is to be taken in its literal sense, not as a figurative usage (majāz). What points to this is His words: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30].

The clarification of this is that His words ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ are explicit that Allah, the Exalted, turns the will and power of the servant, by His own will, toward what His knowledge has already decreed. He turned the will of Pharaoh and his people, by His will, the Exalted, toward picking Moses up, so that he would be for them an enemy and a grief. (p-151) It is as if He says: "We decreed for them to pick him up by Our will, so that he would be for them an enemy and a grief." This is a clear meaning, with no ambiguity or difficulty in it, as you see.

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse: "But if the context is considered, the lām remains a lām of causation, because its meaning is: Allah, the Exalted, предрасположил them to pick him up, so that He would make him an enemy to them and a grief, and this would be more effective in defeating their caution regarding him." The point of his words ends here. This meaning is the verified view regarding the verse, God willing, the Exalted, and His words ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ point to it, as we have explained its aspect a moment ago.

With this verification you know that what many exegetes say, and what they cite poetry to support, namely that the lām in His words "li-yakūna" (so that he might be) is the lām of consequence and outcome (lām al-'āqibah wa-al-ṣayrūrah), is contrary to the correct view. And that what the rhetoricians (al-bayāniyyūn) say, namely that the lām in His words "li-yakūna" contains a dependent metaphor (isti'āra tabaʿiyya) in the object of the meaning of the particle, is also contrary to the correct view.

The explanation of what the rhetoricians mean by this is that among the types of their division of what they call isti'āra (metaphor), which for them is a figurative usage whose relation is similarity, they divide it into an original metaphor (isti'āra aṣliyya) and a dependent metaphor (isti'āra tabaʿiyya). By original metaphor they mean metaphor in non-derived common nouns and verbal nouns (maṣādir). By dependent metaphor they mean two kinds. One of them: metaphor in derived words, such as the active participle (ism al-fā'il) and the verb. The second: metaphor in the object of the meaning of the particle, which is the subject of the clarification here.

The example of original metaphor according to them is: "I saw a lion on his horse." In the word "lion" in this example there is, according to them, an original explicit metaphor (isti'āra aṣliyya taṣrīḥiyya), for he intended to liken the brave man to the lion for the relation of courage. So he omitted the compared element (al-mushabbah), which is the brave man, and stated the comparator (al-mushabbah bihi), which is the lion, by way of explicit metaphor. It became original because "lion" is a non-derived common noun.

The example of dependent metaphor in the derived word according to them is your saying: "The situation is speaking (nāṭiqah) of such-and-such." What they mean is: they liken the indication of the situation to speech, by the common factor of understanding and perception through each of them. So he omitted the indication, which is the compared element, and stated speech, which is the comparator, by way of explicit metaphor, and derived from "speech" the active participle which is "speaking" (nāṭiqah). The dependent metaphor operated in the active participle "speaking." It was called dependent only because it operated in it as a follower of its operation in the verbal noun, which is "speech," since the derived word follows the word from which it is derived, and it cannot be understood without understanding that. This explanation is closer than others that they mention regarding the explanation of what was mentioned.

The example of dependent metaphor according to them in the object of the meaning of the particle, in their claim regarding this noble verse, is that they said: the lām in it is like the word "lion" in the first example, for it was applied to other than the lion because of a resemblance between them. They said: likewise the lām, its origin is laid down to indicate the final cause, and the final cause of a thing is what moves one to attain it so that it occurs after its occurrence. They said: and the final cause of the picking up in His words "So he picked him up" is love, benefit, and adoption, that is, their taking Moses as a son. Just as they stated that this is what motivated them to pick him up and raise him, in His words, exalted, reporting about them: ﴿A comfort of the eye for me and for you; do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [al-Qasas: 9]. So this final cause, according to them, is what moved them to pick him up, so that this cause would be attained for them after the picking up.

They said: and since what actually resulted after the picking up was the opposite of what they hoped and aspired to, namely enmity and grief, the resulting enmity and grief from the picking up were likened to love, adoption, and benefit, which are the final cause of the picking up, by the common factor of the consequence in each of them. The final cause follows its effect always, as a following of hoped-for attainment. So their adoption of Moses and their love for him were what they hoped would follow from picking him up. And since what actually followed from their picking him up was that he would be an enemy to them and a grief, this actual consequence became similar to the hoped-for consequence. Thus the lām that indicates the final cause, which conveys the hoped-for consequence, was borrowed for the actual, factual consequence in which there is no hope.

The clarification of this is that the consequence of grief and enmity from the picking up resembled the consequence of love and adoption from the picking up. So the lām of the final cause was applied to grief and enmity because of their resemblance to adoption and love in the consequence, just as the word "lion" was applied to the brave man because of their resemblance in courage.

Some rhetoricians say: in this, an original metaphor first operated between love and adoption, and between enmity and grief, whose occurrence is the object of the preposition. So the metaphor in the lām was a follower of the metaphor in the object, because the lām does not stand independently, so what is considered in it is a follower of the object, which is the object of the meaning of the particle. Some of them say: the metaphor first operated in causality and purposiveness, and its following in the lām. There are disputes concerning the following in the object of the meaning of the particle which we have left aside, because our aim is only to state their intention regarding the dependent metaphor in this verse, briefly.

(p-153) Since you know their intention by what has been mentioned, know that the verified view, God willing, is what we have put forward. We have also clarified, in our treatise titled "Prohibiting the Permissibility of Figurative Language in the Revealed Text for Worship and Miraculousness" (Man' Jawaz al-Majaz fi al-Munazzal li-al-Ta'abbud wa-al-I'jaz), that the verified view is that there is no figurative language (majāz) in the Qur'an, and we clarified this with clear evidences.

As for His words in this noble verse: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], that is: those who committed the sin (khaṭī'ah), which is the great wrong, like His words: ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned and then made to enter a fire﴾ [Nuh: 25], and His words: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin surrounds him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81], to the end of the verse.

And from the application of "sinner" (khāṭi') to the wrongdoer and disobedient is His words: ﴿Nor any food except from pus, which none eats except the sinners﴾ [al-Haqqah: 36-37], and His words: ﴿a lying, sinful forelock﴾ [al-'Alaq: 16], and His words: ﴿Indeed, you were of the sinners﴾ [Yusuf: 29]. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

(p-361) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said, "[He is] a delight of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him." ﴾ the verse.

The address in His saying "وَلَكَ" (for you, singular) indicates that the one addressed is singular, and in His saying "لا تَقْتُلُوهُ" (do not kill him, plural) it indicates that they are plural.

The answer to this is in three aspects:

First: the form of the plural is used for glorification (ta'ẓīm).

Second: she meant Pharaoh and his helpers who had resolved with him to kill Moses. So she used the singular pronoun in her saying "لَكَ" (for you), because his being "a delight of the eye" in her view belongs to Pharaoh alone, to the exclusion of them. And she used the plural in her saying "لا تَقْتُلُوهُ" (do not kill him), because they were partners with him in the resolve to kill him.

Third: when she sought Pharaoh's compassion for Moses, she turned to those commanded to kill the boys, saying to them: ﴿Do not kill him﴾, giving as the reason her saying: ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us, or we may take him as a son.﴾

This is the commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 28, verse 29:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿He said to his family, "Stay here; indeed, I have perceived a fire"﴾ and the verses that follow. We have already presented its clarification with Qur'anic verses in the surah of "Maryam."

Know that we have sometimes left out many of the verses whose clarification has already been presented, without referring to them, because of how much of their explanation has already preceded.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿He said to his family, "Stay here"﴾ and the verse.

"His family" (ahlihi) means his wife, as evidenced by His statement: ﴿And he set out with his family﴾ [al-Qasas: 29], because it is well known that he set out from the place of Shu'ayb with his wife, the daughter of Shu'ayb or other than Shu'ayb according to that view. And His statement, "Stay here" (imkuthu), is addressed in the masculine plural. So what is the justification for addressing the woman with the masculine plural address?

The answer to this is in three aspects:

The first: a person may address a woman with the plural address out of honor for her, and its parallel is the statement of the poet:

(p-362)

﻿"If you wish, I will forbid women other than you, and if you wish, I will not taste sweet water or cold drink."

The second: that she had a servant with her, and the Arabs sometimes address two persons with the plural address.

The third: that he had with his wife two sons, the name of the elder of them being Gershom (Jirshum), and the name of the younger being Eliezer (al-Ya'zar).

The first answer is evident. The second and third are possibilities, because they are from the Israelite narrations (al-Isra'iliyyat), and knowledge is with God, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 28, verse 42:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made them follow up in this world with a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised.﴾

What Allah, exalted and majestic is He, mentions in this noble verse about His making a curse follow Pharaoh and his soldiers, He also explains in Surah Hud, where He says about them: ﴿And they were made to follow up with a curse in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection. Wretched is the gift that is given.﴾ [Hud: 99]. As for His saying in this noble verse, ﴿among the despised﴾, al-Zamakhshari said: that is, among those who are cast out and distanced. It is not hidden that "al-maqbuhin" is a passive participle (ism maf'ul) of qabbahahu, meaning when he made him ugly (qabih). And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 28, verse 56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, mentions that His Prophet ﷺ does not guide whom he loves to be guided, but rather He, majestic and exalted, is the One who guides whom He wills to guide, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.

This meaning indicated by this verse is clarified in many other verses, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those who misguide﴾ [an-Nahl: 37], and His saying: ﴿And whoever Allah intends for trial, you will not control for him anything from Allah. Those are the ones whose hearts Allah did not intend to purify﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], along with other verses, as its clarification has already passed.

As for His saying: ﴿and He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾, its meaning is clarified in many verses, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾ [an-Najm: 30], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾ [an-Nahl: 125], and the verses of this kind are many. We have previously clarified that the guidance negated from him ﷺ in His saying here: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾, is the guidance of tawfiq (divine enablement, tawfiq), because enablement is in Allah's hand alone; and that the guidance affirmed for him ﷺ in His saying: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [ash-Shura: 52], is the guidance of indication and direction to the truth (dalalah wa irshad). The revelation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾ concerning Abu Talib is well known and famous.

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾.

We have already mentioned that the way to reconcile it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [ash-Shura: 52] is that the guidance negated from him ﷺ is the granting of tawfiq, and the guidance affirmed for him is the making clear of the path.

Allah's statement: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you, except as a mercy from your Lord﴾. We have already presented the verses clarifying this at the beginning of Surat al-Kahf, in the discussion of His statement: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has sent down upon His servant the Book﴾ [al-Kahf: 1].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 28, verse 88:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Everything upon it will perish, and there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman: 26-27]. The "Face" is among the attributes in which one must believe, together with complete transcendence (tanzih) above resemblance to the attributes of creation, as we have clarified in surah "al-A'raf" and elsewhere.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned﴾. We have already presented the verses that clarify this in surah "al-Kahf", in the discussion of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He does not share His authority with anyone﴾ [al-Kahf: 26], and we have left out mention of many cross-references here in surah "al-Qasas".
